blockMcqs.question: What traffic does a service mesh handle, versus an API gateway?
options: Both handle only inbound client traffic
Mesh: service-to-service; gateway: client-to-system
Mesh: client-to-system; gateway: service-to-service
Both handle only internal traffic
blockMcqs.explanation: The mesh owns east-west calls inside; the gateway owns north-south at the edge.

blockMcqs.question: Why reject a bad JWT at the gateway rather than at the service?
options: Services cannot validate tokens at all
It returns 200 faster that way
Bad requests die early, sparing every service
The gateway stores all user passwords
blockMcqs.explanation: Centralized auth fails fast with a 401 before any backend wastes work.

blockMcqs.question: What problem does a BFF solve that a generic gateway doesn't?
options: It terminates TLS for the cluster
It tailors the API shape per client type
It replaces the need for any services
It removes the need for authentication
blockMcqs.explanation: One generic API fits no client perfectly; a BFF shapes data for mobile or web.

blockMcqs.question: How does a sidecar intercept calls without the app knowing?
options: The app imports a mesh SDK
DNS resolves to the control plane
iptables rules redirect traffic to the local proxy
The developer rewrites every request manually
blockMcqs.explanation: Kernel-level iptables quietly route the app's TCP through the local Envoy.

blockMcqs.question: What happens to live traffic if the mesh control plane dies?
options: All service-to-service calls stop immediately
Sidecars keep serving on last-known config
Traffic reroutes through the API gateway
Every pod restarts to recover
blockMcqs.explanation: The control plane only configures sidecars; it is not in the request path.

blockMcqs.question: What is the main runtime cost a service mesh adds?
options: Rewriting application code in Rust
Latency and resources from a proxy per hop
Mandatory loss of mTLS encryption
Forcing all services into one language
blockMcqs.explanation: Each hop traverses two sidecars, adding milliseconds plus memory per pod.

blockMcqs.question: When should you skip a service mesh?
options: When you need zero-trust mTLS everywhere
When you run dozens of polyglot services
With a handful of services or one language
When uniform tracing is a hard requirement
blockMcqs.explanation: At small scale the operational tax outweighs the benefit; a library suffices.

blockMcqs.question: A downstream returns 503; how does the mesh shield the caller?
options: The control plane redeploys the service
The gateway returns a cached response
The sidecar transparently retries another instance
The caller gets the 503 and crashes
blockMcqs.explanation: Retry policy lives in the sidecar, so the caller never sees the transient failure.

blockMcqs.question: Why are unbounded retries dangerous during an outage?
options: They bypass mTLS encryption
They pile load onto a sick service, a retry storm
They disable the control plane
They double the gateway's TLS cost
blockMcqs.explanation: Mass retries amplify traffic to a struggling dependency and deepen the outage.
